name: Curiosity Gap
description: A perceived gap between what someone knows and what they want to know creates an aversive state of deprivation that motivates information-seeking to close it.
design_relevance_note: The theoretical basis for headline/notification copy that withholds a specific detail to drive clicks — and the reason that pattern can tip into manipulative clickbait when overused.
myth_risk_note: Previously rated moderate due to a thin, noisy discovery yield (one on-topic paper found amid heavy contamination from unrelated "information gap" terminology in other fields). Resolved to low: that one paper (Scott 2021) has now been verified and promoted into a real Finding, providing a genuine real-world corpus-linguistic demonstration of the theory in its actual design-practice application (clickbait headlines) -- still no meta-analysis exists, which is why this stays low rather than none.
prevalence_note: A very popular term in content and marketing-copy design circles specifically, less commonly invoked in general UX/product design discourse.

findings.description: Curiosity is best understood not as a stable trait or simple drive, but as a form of cognitively induced deprivation arising from the perceived gap between what a person knows and what they want to know — an 'information gap' account explaining curiosity's characteristic intensity, quick onset, association with impulsivity, and tendency to disappoint once satisfied. Directly explains why deliberately withholding a piece of information (a curiosity gap) drives engagement with headlines, previews, and progress indicators.
findings.source_title: The Psychology of Curiosity: A Review and Reinterpretation

applications.title: Loom hiding what a viewer reaction actually was, only that one exists
applications.description: Loom's video timeline shows that another viewer reacted at a specific moment without revealing what the reaction was, creating an information gap that prompts the current viewer to play that section just to find out -- turning curiosity about a hidden detail into a driver of watch time.
applications.ethical_note: The withheld information here is genuinely trivial (a colleague's reaction to a video) and costs the user nothing beyond a moment's curiosity -- a low-stakes, low-harm illustration, distinct from the Tinder entry in this same wave where a similar information-gap mechanic is used to drive a paid subscription.

applications.title: Tinder Gold blurring the identity of users who already liked your profile
applications.description: Tinder's paid Gold tier reveals that other users have liked your profile, but blurs their photos until you subscribe -- creating an information gap around a socially significant piece of information (who is interested in you) that a free user cannot resolve without paying.
applications.ethical_note: Unlike the Loom entry in this same wave, the withheld information here is socially significant (romantic/social interest) and the discomfort of not knowing is the explicit mechanism used to drive a paywall -- this is a deliberate psychological-discomfort-to-revenue pattern, not an incidental byproduct, and belongs alongside this corpus's existing Dark Patterns & Design Ethics literature on monetizing induced anxiety rather than genuine product value.
